articleTitle: The application of transmission-line modelling to EMC design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: Numerical modeling tools can aid the process of designing for EMC. Transmission-line modelling (TLM) has been successfully applied in a number of EMC applications. The paper outlines the role of modelling in EMC; the features of TLM which suit it to the simulation of EMC problems, some illustrative examples of its application, and future trends.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role of modelling in electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) design and clearance: a user's viewpoint
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: The overwhelming need to ensure sufficient EMC performance at a minimum cost and, in the aerospace industry, weight and volume penalty, necessitates that EMC is considered at the earliest design stage of the product. This simple step of ensuring that EMC is firmly established as part of the design process can reduce the cost of compliance by a factor of five in a military design and development environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Considerations leading to a strategy for the prediction of radiated emissions
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: The authors examine the complexity associated with predicting RFI from a piece of equipment and derive a strategy for dealing with these issues in a sensible time scale with a sufficient degree of accuracy. They discuss whether current techniques are far from fulfilling this task or whether suitably applied, they are actually quite close.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role of TLM in EMC design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: The authors have developed transmission line networks so that the coupling mechanisms in wires and slot apertures can be modelled without having to use a fine mesh. These networks are inserted directly into the TLM mesh at the interface between nodes. TLM has been applied to the study of field ingress into equipment housings, crosstalk problems in circuit interconnections, aircraft simulation in a variety of electromagnetic environments, automobile design, and the EMC testing of ships and military vehicles.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of large electromagnetic computer models in EMC applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: The paper considers the use of computer modelling in EMC applications. It addresses the question 'Why use computer modelling?' and considers the features required of a useful model with reference to well known numerical techniques. The discussion is confined to numerical techniques which are applicable to a wider range of problems than is possible with analytical methods and which provide more quantitative results than knowledge based methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computational modelling for EMC: validation and limitations for practical applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: The use of computational methods is now well established in several important areas of electromagnetic engineering; including antenna design, radar scattering prediction and design for lightning protection. For the majority of EMC applications, however, computational modelling is a comparative newcomer. The paper attempts a realistic assessment of the type of tools the EMC engineer really wants, presents a range of validation results generated within Sowerby Research Centre, and finally identifies a few important outstanding problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Extraction of CAD data for EMC modelling
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: Recent growth in the computational power available at affordable cost has made it practical to carry out significant electromagnetic field analyses by numerical methods. Many other technical areas are feeling the same effect. Fatigue analysis in the automotive industry has been code-of-practice based for many years, but finite element analysis is being used for an increasing minority of components. Solidification analysis of castings has traditionally been based on the Wlodawa modulus back-of-envelope calculations, but finite difference methods are now beginning to be used, even in not-so-large foundries. Structural analysis passed this threshold a decade or so ago, and it may be useful to observe experience in that field.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: EMC modelling, a method for reducing emissions: modelling PCB, cables, and connectors using the Greenfield transmission line simulator from Quantic Laboratories Inc
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Does Electromagnetic Modelling Have a Place in EMC Design
abstract: Greenfield is a field solver utilising boundary element method and transmission line theory for the analysis of high density material interconnect in the time domain. Solving Maxwell equations in homogenous dielectrics utilising Green's function, Greenfield is able to simulate system and subsystem signal integrity design parameters at all stages of the design process. Greenfield models the physical geometry of conductors and dielectric materials, taking into consideration material properties and frequency. Results are presented as transmission line models in the form of inductance, capacitance and resistance matrices. These models can be lossy or lossless. Nonuniform geometry is taken into consideration. Results from the field solver in the form of electrical transmission line models are transferred to Quantic's Spice compatable hybrid network analyser, Phyllis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
